To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the inhibition of angiopoietin signaling by the angiopoietin-1 decoy, exTEK, impairs the growth of both primary and metastatic tumors, and the inhibition is due to a local inflammatory response that is responsible for the impairment of neoangiogenic vessels in the primary tumor, and to a failure in neoangiogenic vessel organization in the metastatic tumor, respectively.

angiopoietin inhibition by soluble exTEK secretions induces an inflammatory response at tumor site and impairment of neo-vessel growth, resulting in tumor growth arrest in subcutis and inhibition of metastases.

(i) exTEK, an angiopoietins decoy, inhibits tumor growth and experimental metastases; (ii) exTEK inhibits angiogenesis in the subcutaneous tumor but not in metastases, where the lack of angiopoietin 1/2 induces inflammation and impairs neoangiogenesis; (iii) the anti-tumor effects of exTEK depend on the presence of a reactive infiltrate and on the antiangiogenic properties of IL-12
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel approach to cancer therapy based on the inhibition of angiopoietin-1 and angiopoietin-TIE2 interaction.
the development of a novel approach for anti-cancer therapy based on angiopoietin blockade.

the development of a therapeutic approach based on the inhibition of angiopoietin activity at the tumor site, which could be used as an adjuvant treatment to reduce the risk of recurrence and metastases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the angiopoietin system is a key player in the tumor-host interaction, and that the inhibition of the angiopoietins by the decoy exTEK can be used as an antiangiogenic strategy to inhibit the growth of primary and metastatic tumor.
angiopoietin inhibition by soluble Tie2 receptor impairs tumor growth, but this effect depends on the tumor site.

the inhibition of angiopoietin signaling by the decoy receptor exTEK induces an inflammatory response that is responsible for the inhibition of tumor growth in the subcutaneous tumor, but not in experimental metastasis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the inhibition of angiopoietin signaling in tumor cells by the exTEK decoy leads to a local inflammatory response that is responsible for the inhibition of subcutaneous tumor growth and for the inhibition of metastases formation.
angiopoietin blockade at tumor site induces an inflammatory response that is responsible for the inhibition of tumor growth and metastatic spread.

1) the extracellular domain of Tie2/TEk (exTEK), when secreted by tumor cells, acts as an angiopoetin decoy, impairing neoangiogenesis in the tumor site and 2) the local inflammatory response induced by exTEK impairs neoangiogenesis in a syngeneiuc model of experimental metastasis, contributing to the inhibition of metastatic growth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
angiopoietins can be targeted to induce anti-angiogenic effects, and this approach can be used in combination with other anti-angiogenic strategies to further limit tumor growth and dissemination.
the inhibition of the angiopoietin/Tie2 axis by the soluble receptor exTEK can induce an anti-tumoral effect, and that the local inflammatory response is a key component of this effect.

the antiangiogenic effect of angiopoietin blockade in the tumor environment may not be limited to inhibition of neoangiogenesis, but may also involve an induction of local inflammation that can hamper tumor growth and metastatic spread.
